headline: Europe's Hidden Snails: Two New Species Discovered in Montenegro
meta_description: Scientists discover two tiny snail species in Montenegro with door-like shells, revealing Europe still holds animals unknown to science.
summary_short: Two newly identified snail species found in Montenegro's mountains have door-like shells and side-mounted eyes—proof that European biodiversity still surprises.
body:
Two tiny snail species unknown to science have been discovered in the mountains of Montenegro, reminding us that even well-studied continents still hold secrets. Named Cochlostoma komarnica and Cochlostoma dobrido, these 6-millimeter cone-shaped creatures possess remarkable features: their eyes sit along the sides of their heads rather than at the tips of stalks, and each carries a circular disk that seals their shell opening like a door when retreating inside. The discovery emerged from expeditions organized between 2018 and 2025 through a partnership involving Taxon Expeditions, the Taxon Foundation, and the Montenegrin Ecologists Society—collaborative work that brought together international researchers, citizen scientists, local students, and conservationists. One participant, musician Janine Buisman from the Netherlands, later became a co-author of the study, having helped collect the specimens during fieldwork in the region's rugged terrain. The snails were named by vote at camp, with one species taking its name from the Dobri Do Plateau in Durmitor National Park and the other from the unprotected Komarnica Canyon.

What makes this discovery particularly poignant is the urgency it reveals. Biologist Jovana Đokić of the Montenegrin Ecologists Society notes that Komarnica Canyon, where one species lives, faces a genuine threat: a proposed hydropower dam would flood the canyon and destroy its entire ecosystem before science has fully documented what lives there. Conservation groups are now racing to survey the canyon's biodiversity, building a case for its protection. Đokić argues that a UNESCO World Heritage designation and abandonment of the hydropower project are essential. The snails themselves feed on algae and lichens on limestone rocks, thriving in an environment that took decades to properly study—a reminder that protecting wild places matters not just for known species, but for the countless undiscovered ones waiting in the shadows.
quick_facts: Two new snail species discovered in Montenegro, each 6 mm long
Expeditions ran 2018–2025 with citizen scientists and local collaborators
Shells close like doors with circular disk seals
Komarnica Canyon species threatened by proposed hydropower dam
